items.title: Updating last prices
items.prose: A feed sends 1,000,000 ticks a day across 5,000 tickers. Each tick updates that ticker's last price. Version A keeps a list of `(ticker, price)` pairs and scans it for the ticker. Version B keeps a dict keyed by ticker.
items.question: Roughly how much work does each version do in a day?

options.text: A: about $2.5 \times 10^9$ comparisons. B: about $10^6$ hash lookups.
A: about $2.5 \times 10^9$ comparisons. B: about the same, since a dict also searches its keys.
options.why: You treated the dict as a scan. It hashes the ticker straight to a bucket, so a lookup costs $O(1)$ on average.

options.text: A: about $10^6$ comparisons. B: about $10^6$ hash lookups.
options.why: You counted one step per tick for the list. A scan reads about half of the 5,000 pairs on each tick.

options.text: A: about $2.5 \times 10^9$ comparisons. B: about $10^6 \times \log_2 5{,}000$ steps.
options.why: You costed a sorted list or a tree. A hash map does no halving: one bucket per lookup on average.

feedback.correct: The scan costs about 2,500 comparisons a tick; the dict about one lookup.
feedback.generic: Count the work per tick for each version, then multiply by 1,000,000 ticks.

explain.text: A scan finds a random ticker after about $5{,}000/2 = 2{,}500$ comparisons. Over $10^6$ ticks that is $2.5 \times 10^9$. The dict hashes each ticker once, so the day costs about $10^6$ lookups.

items.title: Who is hit next
items.prose: Each node is a bank, and each edge a large exposure between two banks. Bank A defaults. We run breadth-first search from A, adding neighbours in alphabetical order.

state.caption: Processed so far: A, then B

items.question: Tap the bank that BFS processes next.

feedback.correct: C joined the queue before D and E, so it comes out next.
feedback.generic: A queue serves first come, first served. Which bank joined the queue first after B?

byKey.D: D was found from B, two edges from A. C, one edge from A, joined the queue earlier.
byKey.E: E was found from B, two edges from A. C joined the queue earlier, from A.
byKey.F: F is found only when C is processed. It is not in the queue yet.
byKey.G: G is three edges from A. BFS finishes every closer bank first.
byKey.A: A has already been processed. Its badge shows 1.
byKey.B: B has already been processed. Its badge shows 2.

items.title: Netting two trades
items.prose: We look for two trade sizes in this sorted list that add to 34 lots. `i` starts at the left end and `j` at the right. A sum that is too small moves `i` right; a sum that is too big moves `j` left.
items.question: Tap the two cells compared on the scan's fourth comparison.

feedback.correct: The fourth comparison is $11 + 24 = 35$.
feedback.generic: Write each sum and the pointer it moves: 33, then 38, then 32, then the fourth.

byKey.rule-swapped: You moved `j` when the sum was too small. A smaller sum needs a bigger left value, so `i` moves.
byKey.third: That is the third comparison, $8 + 24 = 32$. It is too small, so `i` moves once more.
byKey.final: That is the pair that nets, $15 + 19 = 34$, found on the sixth comparison.

explain.text: $3 + 30 = 33$ is small, so `i` moves. $8 + 30 = 38$ is big, so `j` moves. $8 + 24 = 32$ is small, so the fourth sum is $11 + 24 = 35$.

items.title: Finding 14:30 in a day of ticks
items.prose: A day's 1,000,000 ticks are sorted by timestamp. Binary search finds the first tick at or after 14:30:00. Each probe reads one tick and halves the range left.
items.question: At most how many probes does it need?

feedback.correct: Twenty halvings cut a million ticks down to one place.
feedback.generic: Find the smallest $k$ with $2^k$ at least the number of places the answer could be.

byKey.floor: $2^{19} = 524{,}288$ is short of a million places. One more halving is needed.
byKey.log10: You used $\log_{10}$. Each probe halves the range, so count powers of 2.
byKey.half: That is a scan's average. Binary search halves the range on every probe.
byKey.linear: That is a scan from the first tick. Binary search halves the range on every probe.

explain.text: After $k$ probes about $10^6/2^k$ places remain. $2^{19} = 524{,}288$ is too few and $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ is enough. So 20 probes always suffice.

items.title: Undoing amendments
items.prose: A trading screen keeps an undo stack of order ids. It holds 101, 102 and 103, with 103 on top. Then come: pop, push 104, pop, pop, push 105.
items.question: Which ids are left, listed bottom first?

options.why: You took ids off the bottom, as a queue does. A stack pops the newest id first.
You stopped after two pops. The third pop, after 104 goes, takes 102.
Five ids went in and three came out, so two remain. 101 never left the bottom.

feedback.correct: The pops take 103, then 104, then 102.
feedback.generic: Apply the operations one by one. Each pop removes the id on top.

explain.text: Pop takes 103. Push 104, then pop takes 104 and the next pop takes 102. Push 105 leaves 101 and 105.

items.title: A new ask joins the heap
items.prose: Ask prices in pence sit in a min-heap stored as a list. The parent of index `i` is at index `(i - 1) // 2`. A new ask at 102p has just been appended at index 10.

state.caption: 102 has just been appended at index 10

items.question: After it sifts up, at which index does 102 rest?

feedback.correct: 102 swaps past 104 and 103, then stops below 100.
feedback.generic: Compare 102 with its parent and swap while the parent is larger.

byKey.half-parent: You took the parent of `i` as `i // 2`. With index 0 as the root, it is `(i - 1) // 2`.
byKey.one-swap: You stopped after one swap. At index 4 its parent is 103 at index 1, still larger.
byKey.no-sift: A push must restore the heap. 102 is smaller than its parent, 104, so it moves up.
byKey.root: 100 at the root is smaller than 102, so 102 stops just below it.

explain.text: Index 10's parent is index 4, holding 104: swap. Index 4's parent is index 1, holding 103: swap. Index 1's parent holds 100, which is smaller, so 102 stays at index 1.

items.title: A loop that doubles its step
items.prose:
This function sums some prices for every day of a list of $n$ prices.

```python
def scan(prices):
    n = len(prices)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        step = 1
        while step < n:
            total += prices[(i + step) % n]
            step *= 2
    return total
```
items.question: What is its running time in big O?

options.why: You saw two nested loops. The inner one doubles `step`, so it runs about $\log_2 n$ times, not $n$.
You counted only the inner loop. The outer loop still runs it once for each of the $n$ days.
The inner loop's count grows with $n$: about $\log_2 n$ passes for each day.

feedback.correct: $n$ outer passes, each with about $\log_2 n$ inner steps.
feedback.generic: Count how many values `step` takes before it reaches $n$, then multiply by the outer loop.

explain.text: `step` runs through 1, 2, 4, and so on below $n$: about $\log_2 n$ values. The outer loop repeats that $n$ times. For $n = 1{,}000$ that is 10,000 additions, not 1,000,000.

items.title: Storing an exposure network
items.prose: A counterparty network has 5,000 firms and 20,000 two-way exposures. As adjacency lists, each exposure appears in both firms' lists. As a matrix, there is one cell for every ordered pair of firms.
items.question: How many times as many entries does the matrix hold as the lists?

feedback.correct: 25,000,000 cells against 40,000 list entries.
feedback.generic: Count the matrix cells, $n^2$. Then count the list entries: two per exposure.

byKey.once: You counted each exposure once. A two-way exposure sits in both firms' lists: 40,000 entries.
byKey.upper: You kept only half the matrix. The question counts every ordered pair, all $5{,}000^2$ cells.
byKey.nodes: You divided by the number of firms. Divide by the number of list entries.

explain.text: The matrix has $5{,}000^2 = 25{,}000{,}000$ cells. The lists hold $2 \times 20{,}000 = 40{,}000$ entries. The ratio is 625, so a sparse network belongs in lists.

items.title: Newest tick first
items.prose: A script builds a list of 1,000 ticks, newest first, with `ticks.insert(0, t)` for each tick. Each insert shifts every value already in the list one place right.
items.question: How many shifts do the 1,000 inserts make in total?

feedback.generic: The $k$-th insert finds $k - 1$ values already there. Add those up.

byKey.square: You charged $n$ shifts to every insert. The list starts empty and grows by one each time.
byKey.plus-one: You added 1 to 1,000. The first insert shifts nothing and the last shifts 999.
byKey.one-each: Each insert shifts the whole list so far, not one value.

explain.text: The inserts shift $0, 1, 2, \dots, 999$ values. That sums to $999 \times 1{,}000/2 = 499{,}500$: quadratic. Appending and reversing once, or `deque.appendleft`, is linear.

items.title: Settling venues by latency
items.prose: Edges are two-way links between data centres, labelled with their latency in milliseconds. Dijkstra's algorithm runs from LDN.
items.question: Put the venues in the order Dijkstra settles them.

feedback.correct: LDN 0, AMS 2, PAR 3, FRA 4, ZRH 7, MIL 9.
feedback.generic: Each round settles the unsettled venue with the lowest known latency. Then update its neighbours.

byKey.FRA: FRA is one hop from LDN but 4 ms away. AMS at 2 ms and PAR at 3 ms settle first.
byKey.MIL: MIL is 10 ms via PAR but 9 ms via FRA and ZRH. It settles last.
byKey.ZRH: ZRH is reached only through FRA, at 4 + 3 = 7 ms.

explain.text: From LDN the frontier is AMS 2, PAR 3 and FRA 4, settled in that order. FRA then offers ZRH at 7, and ZRH offers MIL at 9, beating 10 via PAR.

items.title: Two fills that make 30 lots
items.prose: A client wants 30 lots matched by exactly two of these fills. One pass keeps a dict `seen` from size to index. At each fill it looks up `30 - size` in `seen`, then stores the fill if there is no match.
items.question: Fill in what each step looks up, and whether it finds it.

feedback.correct: Index 3 finds 12 in `seen` and returns indices 0 and 3.
feedback.generic: Look up first, then store. `seen` holds only the fills before the current one.

byKey.r0c3: `seen` is empty at index 0, so nothing can be found.
byKey.r2c3: 5 is in the list, but at index 4, after 25. At index 2, `seen` holds only 12 and 7.
byKey.r3c3: At index 3 `seen` holds 12, 7 and 25. The lookup for 12 succeeds.

explain.text: The lookups are 18, 23, 5 and 12. Only 12 is already stored, from index 0. The pass returns $(0, 3)$ before it ever reaches the pair 25 and 5.

items.title: Quicksort on sorted timestamps
items.prose: A quicksort always takes the first element as its pivot. Each partition compares the pivot with every other element of its part. It is given 12 trade timestamps that are already in order.
items.question: How many comparisons does it make in total?

feedback.correct: $11 + 10 + \dots + 1 = 66$, the worst case.
feedback.generic: On sorted input the pivot is the smallest value. What is left for the next partition?

byKey.nlogn: $n \log_2 n \approx 43$ is the good case, with balanced splits. Sorted input with a first pivot splits off nothing.
byKey.square: You charged 12 comparisons to each of 12 partitions. The parts shrink by one each time.
byKey.triangle: You counted $12 + 11 + \dots + 1$. A part of size $m$ needs $m - 1$ comparisons.
byKey.double: You counted each comparison twice. The pivot meets each other element once.

explain.text: The first pivot is the smallest, so the split is empty and 11. The parts shrink by one each round: $11 + 10 + \dots + 1 = 66$. A random pivot makes this case unlikely.

items.title: The overnight risk run
items.prose: An arrow from one job to another means the first must finish before the second starts. Kahn's algorithm has emitted its first round: rates, prices and positions.
items.question: Tap every job that is ready to run now.

feedback.correct: curves and fx have nothing left to wait for.
feedback.generic: A job is ready when every arrow into it starts at a job that has run.

byKey.one-parent: VaR has one input done, positions, but not all. It still waits for greeks.
byKey.greeks: greeks waits for curves and fx. Neither has run yet.
byKey.var: VaR has positions, but it still waits for greeks.
byKey.report: report waits for greeks and VaR. Neither has run.
byKey.prices: prices has already run in the first round.
byKey.rates: rates has already run in the first round.
byKey.positions: positions has already run in the first round.

explain.text: Removing the first round drops the in-degrees of curves and fx to 0. VaR keeps its arrow from greeks, which has not run. So the second round is curves and fx.

items.title: A run with few losing days
items.prose: These are a desk's daily P&L figures in £k. Risk wants the longest run of consecutive days with at most two losing days. A sliding window grows on the right and shrinks on the left when a third loss joins.
items.question: How many days long is the longest such run?

feedback.correct: Days 5 to 11 hold seven days with two losses.
feedback.generic: Move the left edge just past the oldest loss whenever a third loss enters.

byKey.restart: You restarted the window at each third loss. Drop only the oldest loss, so the other two can stay.
byKey.no-loss: That is the longest run with no losses. Two losing days are allowed.
byKey.all: The whole list has five losing days. Only two are allowed.

explain.text: The losses fall at indices 1, 3, 4, 7 and 10. A window may hold two of them. The best spans from just after index 4 to the end: indices 5 to 11, seven days.

items.title: A recursive P&L total
items.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: The base case is correct: an empty list sums to 0.

options.why: Each call holds a frame and a fresh slice. The frames alone are $O(n)$, and the live slices add up to $O(n^2)$.
A list cannot be a cache key, so `lru_cache` raises `TypeError`. Nothing repeats here anyway.

feedback.correct: Slices cost $O(n^2)$ copying, and the depth is one frame per day.
feedback.generic: Count what `pnl[1:]` copies on each call, and how many frames are open at once.

explain.text: `pnl[1:]` copies $n - 1$, then $n - 2$ values, and so on: about $n^2/2$ in all. Each call waits for the next, so 5,000 days need 5,000 frames. A loop, or `sum(pnl)`, fixes both.

items.title: Hedges under a margin budget
items.prose: Three hedges use margin and cut risk. A: £2m margin, 3 units of risk cut. B: £3m, 4 units. C: £4m, 6 units. Each is taken whole or not at all. Cell (row, budget) holds the best cut using the hedges up to that row.
items.question: The cell marked ? is filled from two cells. Tap both.

feedback.correct: Skip C: 7. Take C: $3 + 6 = 9$. The cell is 9.
feedback.generic: Either C is skipped, or it is taken and uses £4m of the £6m. Both read the row above.

byKey.same-row: You read row +C at budget 2. That row may already contain C, so C could be taken twice.
byKey.minus-one: You stepped back one column. Taking C uses its £4m of margin, so step back 4.
byKey.r4c7: That is the cell being filled. Tap the two it reads from.
byKey.r4c6: That is in row +C, which may already hold C. Read the row above.

explain.text: Skipping C leaves the best with A and B at £6m: 7. Taking C leaves £2m for A and B: $3 + 6 = 9$. The cell takes the larger, 9.

items.title: Cancelling a resting order
items.prose: One price level holds resting orders in time priority. The oldest fills first. Cancels arrive by order id, and each must cost $O(1)$.
items.question: Which design keeps fills in order and makes every cancel $O(1)$?

options.text: A doubly linked list of orders, plus a dict from order id to its node
A singly linked list of orders, plus a dict from order id to its node
options.why: Unlinking a node changes its predecessor's `next`. A singly linked node does not know its predecessor, so you walk from the head.

options.text: A Python list in time order, with `orders.remove(order_id)`
options.why: `remove` scans for the id and then shifts every later order left: $O(n)$.

options.text: A min-heap keyed by arrival time
options.why: A heap finds the oldest order fast, but it cannot find an arbitrary id without a search.

feedback.correct: The dict finds the node, and the node's two links unlink it.
feedback.generic: A cancel must find the order and remove it, both without a scan.

explain.text: The dict jumps to the node in $O(1)$ on average. The node knows both neighbours, so joining them unlinks it in $O(1)$. The head of the list is still the oldest order.

items.title: Booking one execution slot
items.prose: One execution algorithm can work one client order at a time. Each order needs it from its start to its end, in minutes after the open. An order may start at the minute another ends.
items.question: At most how many orders can the algorithm work?

feedback.correct: O2, O4, O6 and O7, by earliest end first.
feedback.generic: Take the order that ends first, drop every order it clashes with, and repeat.

byKey.earliest-start: You took the earliest start first. O1 starts first but runs 45 minutes and blocks three orders.
byKey.shortest: You took the shortest first. O5 is short but sits across O4 and O6, which together beat it.
byKey.all: Several orders overlap. The slot works one order at a time.

explain.text: Earliest end first takes O2 (ends 30), O4 (30 to 45), O6 (45 to 60) and O7. Finishing first always leaves the most room for the rest. That is why this greedy rule is safe.

items.title: Cutting off dead hedges
items.prose: A search picks hedges A (£4m), B (£3m) and C (£2m), taking (+) or skipping each in turn. The budget is £5m. The search abandons a branch as soon as its cost passes £5m. Leaves show each full choice's cost.
items.question: Tap every branch where the search stops because the cost has passed £5m.

feedback.correct: The search cuts at +A then +B, and at +A, skip B, +C.
feedback.generic: Walk down each path adding costs. Stop at the first branch where the total passes £5m.

byKey.leaves: You marked the leaves over budget. The search stops at +A, +B, already £7m, and never reaches the two leaves below.
byKey.five: +B and +C cost exactly £5m. That is within budget, so the search goes on.
byKey.y-y-y: The search never gets here. It stopped one level up, at £7m.
byKey.y-y-n: The search never gets here. It stopped one level up, at £7m.
byKey.n-y-y: £3m plus £2m is £5m, which is within budget.

explain.text: +A and +B is £7m, so the search cuts there and skips both leaves below. +A, skip B, +C is £6m, another cut. Every other path stays at or under £5m.

widget.solution:
def lifo_pnl(trades):
    """trades: (side, qty, price) tuples in time order.
    side is "B" or "S"; price is in pence.
    A sale closes the most recent open buys first.
    Return the realised P&L in pence."""
    lots = []  # open buys as [qty, price], newest last
    pnl = 0
    for side, qty, price in trades:
        if side == "B":
            lots.append([qty, price])
            continue
        while qty > 0:
            top = lots[-1]          # the newest open buy
            take = min(qty, top[0])
            pnl += take * (price - top[1])
            top[0] -= take
            qty -= take
            if top[0] == 0:
                lots.pop()
    return pnl

feedback.correct: Your open lots behave as a stack: the newest buy closes first.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. A sale takes from `lots[-1]`, and splits it when the sale is smaller.

byKey.test-1: Selling 100 at 530p closes the buy at 520p, the newest: 1,000p, not 3,000p.
byKey.test-4: A sale of 150 takes 100 at 520p, then 50 of the 500p lot.
byKey.test-6: A sale of 250 takes the 450p and 420p lots whole, then 50 of the 400p lot.

explain.text: The open lots are a stack: a buy pushes, a sale takes from the top. A partial take shrinks the top lot and leaves it there. FIFO would use a queue instead and book a different P&L.

items.prose: `ts` holds fill times in seconds, sorted. `L(x)` is `bisect_left(ts, x)`: the first index whose value is at least `x`. `R(x)` is `bisect_right(ts, x)`: the first index whose value is above `x`.
items.question: Fill in each value.

feedback.correct: A closed range is `R(15) - L(7)`; a half-open one is `L(15) - L(8)`.
feedback.generic: Find each boundary index on the strip. A count is the difference of two boundaries.

byKey.r1c1: The last 7 is at index 3, so the first value above 7 is at index 4.
byKey.r3c1: Both 15s come before index 7, where 20 sits.
byKey.r4c1: Count from the first 7, index 1, up to just past the last 15, index 7.

items.prose: A desk's daily P&L is in whole pence. We want the longest run of consecutive days whose P&L sums to exactly zero. For `[5, -3, -2, 4, 1]` that is $-3, -2, 4, 1$: four days.

widget.solution:
def longest_flat(pnl):
    """pnl: daily P&L in whole pence.
    Return the length of the longest run of consecutive
    days that sums to exactly 0, or 0 if there is none."""
    first = {0: -1}   # running total -> first day it was seen
    total = 0
    best = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(pnl):
        total += x
        if total in first:
            best = max(best, i - first[total])
        else:
            first[total] = i
    return best

tests.setup: import random; random.seed(81); pnl = [random.randint(-40, 60) for _ in range(100000)]

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, compared with ==. Tests 8 to 10 have 100,000 days each. Trying every start and end is quadratic and runs out of time. The first run starts Python in your browser, which can take 10 to 20 seconds. Later runs are quick.

feedback.correct: Two equal running totals bracket a zero-sum run, and the dict keeps the earliest.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Store the first day each running total appears, and seed the dict with total 0 at day −1.

byKey.test-3: `[0]` is one flat day. A run starting at day 0 needs total 0 recorded before day 0.
byKey.test-5: `[3, -3, 3, -3]` is flat over all four days. Keep the first index of each total, never a later one.
byKey.test-9: No run of 1s sums to zero, so the answer is 0.
byKey.error: If it stopped at the time limit, you try every start. Use running totals and a dict for one pass.

explain.text: Equal running totals after days $i$ and $j$ mean days $i + 1$ to $j$ sum to zero. A dict from total to its first day finds the longest such gap in one pass. Recording total 0 at day −1 covers runs that start on day 0.

items.title: Three calls on halves
items.prose: A risk routine splits $n$ positions in half and makes three recursive calls on halves. It then does $n$ steps of combining. So $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n$, with $T(1) = 1$. A run on 1,024 positions takes 1 second.
items.question: About how many seconds does a run on 4,096 positions take?

widget.label: Seconds
widget.accept: About 9 s (9.06 exactly from the recurrence)

feedback.correct: Quadrupling $n$ multiplies the work by about $3^2 = 9$.
feedback.generic: Draw the recursion tree. Which level costs most: the top, or the leaves?

byKey.nlogn: That is $n \log n$ growth, from two calls on halves. Three calls make the leaves dominate.
byKey.square: That is $n^2$ growth, from four calls on halves.
byKey.linear: You scaled with the top level's $n$. Each level down costs 1.5 times the one above.
byKey.three: You applied the factor 3 once. 4,096 is two halvings further than 1,024: $3 \times 3$.

explain.text: Level $k$ of the tree costs $(3/2)^k n$, so the $3^{\log_2 n} = n^{\log_2 3}$ leaves dominate. Two more halvings multiply the leaves by $3^2 = 9$. The exact ratio, $T(4096)/T(1024)$, is 9.06.

items.title: Trading with a fee
items.prose: You may hold at most one share and trade as often as you like. Each sale costs a fixed fee. Prices are daily closes in pence. For `[1, 3, 2, 8, 4, 9]` with fee 2, the best is buy 1, sell 8, buy 4, sell 9: 8p.
items.question: Write `max_profit(prices, fee)`: the best total profit in pence, 0 if no trade pays.

widget.starter:
def max_profit(prices, fee):
    """prices: daily closes in pence. Hold at most one share.
    Buy and sell as often as you like; each sale pays fee pence.
    Return the best total profit in pence, 0 if no trade pays."""
    ...
widget.solution:
def max_profit(prices, fee):
    """prices: daily closes in pence. Hold at most one share.
    Buy and sell as often as you like; each sale pays fee pence.
    Return the best total profit in pence, 0 if no trade pays."""
    if not prices:
        return 0
    flat = 0              # best P&L so far, holding nothing
    held = -prices[0]     # best P&L so far, holding one share
    for p in prices[1:]:
        flat, held = max(flat, held + p - fee), max(held, flat - p)
    return flat

tests.setup:

for _ in range(99999): px.append(px[-1] + random.randint(-25, 25))

items.title: Deleting a price level
items.prose: Price levels in pence sit in a binary search tree. We delete 50, which has two children. The code replaces a node like this with its in-order successor, then removes the successor from its old place.

feedback.correct: 55 moves up to the root, and 57 takes 55's old place under 60.

items.title: At most two round trips

feedback.correct: Buy at 5, sell at 16, buy at 13, sell at 18: $11 + 5 = 16$.
feedback.generic: Split the days at every point. Take the best single trade on each side and add them.

byKey.unlimited: That adds every rise: four trips. Only two are allowed.

explain.text: Split the eight days at each point and add the best trade on each side. Splitting at the 16 gives $(16 - 5) + (18 - 13) = 16$. The greedy best trade, 5 to 18, blocks that better pair.

items.title: Designing an order book
items.model:
**(a)** For each side we keep three things.

- A dict from price to a **level**. A level holds its orders in a doubly linked list, oldest at the head, and its total quantity.
- A dict from order id to its list node. This finds any order without a search.
- A heap of the side's live prices: a max-heap for bids (store $-p$) and a min-heap for asks. Its top is the best price.

The list gives time priority within a level. The heap gives price priority across levels.

**(b)** Let $L$ be the live levels on a side, about 500.

- *Add.* Find the level in the price dict, $O(1)$ on average. Append the node at the tail, $O(1)$. A new price also pushes onto the heap: $O(\log L)$, about 9 steps.
- *Cancel.* The id dict finds the node in $O(1)$. Its two links unlink it in $O(1)$, and the level's quantity drops. A singly linked list would need a walk to the predecessor.
- *Best bid or ask.* Peek at the heap's top: $O(1)$, once dead levels are cleared (part c).
- *Match.* Take from the best level's head, filling oldest first. Each fill is $O(1)$. An emptied level is popped from the heap in $O(\log L)$. A market order that makes $k$ fills across $m$ levels costs $O(k + m \log L)$.

So nearly every message is $O(1)$, and only level changes pay $O(\log L)$. At a million messages a day that is trivial work.

**(c)** A heap cannot delete an arbitrary price cheaply. When a cancel empties a level, we drop it from the price dict. Its price stays in the heap. That is **lazy deletion**. Before reading the best price, we pop tops whose level is gone. Each dead price is popped once, so the cost is $O(\log L)$ amortised per level ever created. A live price must not be pushed twice. So we push only when the price dict lacks it.

**(d)** Prices sit inside a 200-tick band. So use an **array of 401 levels**, indexed by tick offset from a base price. Add and cancel stay $O(1)$, with no hashing of prices. Keep an index of the best occupied tick. After a fill or cancel empties it, scan outwards to the next occupied tick. That scan is at most 400 steps and usually one or two. The array also gives depth at any price in $O(1)$ and is cache-friendly. If the band moves, re-centre the base, which costs $O(\text{band})$ but is rare.

**Summary.** Dicts give $O(1)$ lookup by price and by id. Doubly linked lists give FIFO fills and $O(1)$ unlinks. A heap with lazy deletion, or a bounded tick array, gives the best price.

rubric.text: Per price level, a FIFO structure (a doubly linked list or deque) giving time priority, with a total quantity.
A dict from order id to node, and explains why a doubly linked node makes cancel $O(1)$.
A heap or balanced tree of prices gives the best bid and ask. A new level costs $O(\log L)$; a peek costs $O(1)$.
Costs matching: $O(k + m \log L)$ for $k$ fills over $m$ levels, oldest order first.
Lazy deletion: dead prices stay in the heap and are popped before a read, amortised $O(\log L)$.
For a bounded band, an array indexed by tick with a best-tick index, and justifies $O(1)$ add and cancel.

explain.text: Each job gets its own structure: dicts find, linked lists keep time order, and a heap or array keeps price order. The design is judged by its worst common operation. Here that is the cancel, which must be $O(1)$.
